title: Asynchronous Baton Scheduler for heterogeneous tensor/pipeline handovers
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary:
We need a new multi-GPU handover mechanism that minimizes tail latency and NCCL contention across heterogeneous device groups while preserving deterministic kernel selection heuristics. The proposed Asynchronous Baton Scheduler (ABS) hands off token prefill/short-decode work using compact "baton" metadata so downstream stages can proceed early or defer with minimal synchronization.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Current synchronous handoffs create bursty NCCL traffic spikes when many tokens converge at stage boundaries, causing tail latency regressions under mixed workloads.
- Static token batching and purely topology-aware routing can't adapt quickly to transient load imbalances across tensor/pipeline parallel groups.
- Kernel selection logic currently assumes stable sequence-length distributions; unexpected handoff timing changes can force suboptimal kernels or extra kernel switches.

Goals / success metrics:
- Reduce 99th percentile prefill+decode latency by 20% for heterogeneous GPU pools under mixed short/long sequence workloads.
- Reduce NCCL allreduce/allgather peak concurrency by 25% (measured as concurrent NCCL endpoints active per second) in stress tests.
- Keep additional CPU overhead <5% on conductor and keep code changes isolated to orchestration and handoff layers.

Design overview:
- Baton concept: compact metadata packet attached to a token microbatch that contains (approx) token range, KV-cache hint, preferred kernel-tag, and an adaptive earliness score. The baton is small (<=128 bytes) to reduce network effect.
- Asynchronous handoff: upstream stage sends batons immediately when a microbatch is prefilled; downstream stages make local decisions to accept, delay, or request partial prefetch based on current backlog, device temperature, and estimated kernel cost.
- Opportunistic early-decode: if downstream has idle cycles and kernel-tag matches, it will start decode early using local KV-hint (best-effort), reducing end-to-end latency. 
- Deferred aggregation window: when many batons arrive, downstream forms micro-windows to coalesce NCCL ops and avoid massive concurrency spikes. Windows are size/adaptive and can be 0 (pass-through) to N tokens.
- Kernel reconciliation: before executing heavy kernels (e.g., fused attention variants), stages exchange a tiny kernel-consensus bit via baton acknowledgement. If consensus differs, the conductor triggers a lightweight re-evaluation and may fall back to a conservative kernel choice for affected microbatches.

Algorithm steps (simplified):
1) Upstream prefill finishes microbatch -> emit baton with hints.
2) Baton routed via smart-router to downstream replica set instead of waiting for full microbatch.
3) Downstream checks local heuristics: backlog, idle-CPU, device throughput, current NCCL concurrency.
4a) If idle and kernel-tag compatible -> early-decode path using cached KV-hint.
4b) If busy but small backlog -> accept baton and schedule standard execute.
4c) If transient overload detected -> defer and join a deferred aggregation window; signal upstream to reroute or slow prefill.
5) When window closes, coalesced NCCL ops executed to reduce concurrency spikes.
6) Kernel-consensus step executed pre-heavy-kernel. If mismatch, mark microbatch for conservative path and emit telemetry.

Trade-offs considered:
- Increased orchestration complexity vs. latency reduction: ABS adds negotiation overhead but keeps heavy NCCL ops coordinated.
- Risk of KV-cache divergence when relying on early-decode hints: mitigated by conservative fallbacks and checksum validation.
- Additional metadata (baton) increases network chatter but is intentionally limited in size.

Instrumentation & telemetry:
- New gauges: baton-rate (batons/s), baton-accept-rate, early-decode-success-rate, deferred-window-size distribution, kernel-consensus-failures.
- NCCL concurrency heatmap per topology and per minute.
- Traces: end-to-end token lifecycle with baton events annotated (emit span tags).
- Success dashboards: 99/95/50 latency curves for prefill+decode, peak NCCL endpoints, and kernel-switch rate.

Testing plan:
- Microbenchmarks: synthetic short/long workload mixes across heterogeneous devices (A10032GB + A10040GB + H100 variants) to validate tail-latency and NCCL concurrency.
- Chaos tests: transient slow device, sudden spike of short sequences, and simulated network jitter to ensure robust defer/retry.
- Determinism test: seed-based runs to ensure kernel reconciliation doesn't introduce non-determinism in outputs beyond known tolerances.
- Integration tests: run on staging Dedicated cluster with traffic replay from production traces.

Rollout plan:
- Stage 1 (canary): ABS disabled by default; enable per-customer flag for 5% of traffic on staging cluster. Verify telemetry and kernel-consensus failures <0.1% and tail latency improvement.
- Stage 2 (gradual): Ramp to 25% on dedicated pools with mixed device types and enable automatic deferred-window heuristics.
- Stage 3 (opt-in release): Expose ABS toggle in Dedicated config and Redwood Console with recommended defaults; enable for select customers.
- Stage 4: Default enabled with conservative heuristics and monitoring alarms.

Rollback criteria:
- >10% increase in 99th pct latency in production for more than 5 minutes.
- NCCL concurrency spike above historical 3-sigma sustained for >2 minutes.
- Kernel-consensus-failures exceeding 1% over 15 minutes.

Dependencies:
- Smart-router feature flags and routing policy hooks (ENG-202010 - dependency).
- Kernel-tag propagation plumbing in runtime (ENG-220915 - dependency).
- Telemetry backend support for new gauges and heatmaps (OBS-134 - dependency).

Open questions / risks:
- How to pick window sizing heuristics under extremely bursty workloads without adding oscillation? Proposed approach: PID-inspired damped adjustments with minimum and max caps.
- Is 128 bytes baton budget acceptable for all private deployments? Consider config knob for enterprise networks.
- Interaction with quantized kernels and fallback to unquantized kernels—need explicit test matrix.

Implementation milestones:
- Week 1: proto baton data-structure, conductor APIs, small router hooks, unit tests.
- Week 2: early-decode path and KV-hint validation code, unit tests.
- Week 3: deferred-window mechanism + NCCL coalescing primitives, integration tests.
- Week 4: kernel-consensus step, telemetry, staging rollout.
